header.scope: Only memberships and online billing were signed. Studio front-desk processing is phase two with no date, and Global Payments still handles it today.
header.tag_why: Greg, the controller, sat on the paper for two weeks and said nothing in two meetings. After Tobi ran one month of Corelane's own failed renewals, Greg asked for the spreadsheet and the deal signed four days later. The rep's read is that this was the moment, but the rep also thought they were only there to keep the incumbent honest. Global's longer-contract bundle and Greg's termination-fee questions are the runner-up.

messaging_changes.current_line: Recover failed payments automatically with smart retries.
messaging_changes.change: Lead with a customer-specific proof offer: "Send us one month of your failed renewals and we'll show which ones come back with a retry or an updated card. Your file, not our average."
messaging_changes.why: The generic retry claim is what every vendor says. The only moment that moved the silent economic decision-maker was a view built from the customer's own data, and the signature came four days later.
evidence_excerpts: Specifically when our solutions engineer, Tobi, took an export of one month of their failed renewals and showed which ones were the kind that usually come back with a retry or an updated card.
Greg hadn't said a word in two meetings, and he asked for the spreadsheet.

messaging_changes.current_line: Online and in-store on one platform; the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
messaging_changes.change: Replace the abstract 'unified commerce' framing with a concrete front-desk claim (member check-in and a retail sale on one screen in their studio software). Use it only once it can be shown working in the customer's own setup.
messaging_changes.why: The buyer heard 'unified commerce' as a hardware question. The real test was a single-screen front desk, which we could only show through a partner demo, and phase two depends on that integration.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: For subscription and membership buyers, open on the problem they named (members lost to failed cards, not to a decision to leave) instead of the global slide.
messaging_changes.why: The global opener drew silence from a buyer with US and Canada footprint. The problem Maya raised from her board deck was failed-card churn.
evidence_excerpts: I opened with the global slide. They have studios in the US and a handful in Canada.
members who never meant to leave.

messaging_changes.change: Add a short, plain answer on contract term and cost to leave, ready before the evaluation reaches the controller.
messaging_changes.why: After Global's rate review and bundle, the finance questions shifted to term and exit cost. We have no message for the lock-in worry.
evidence_excerpts: Greg asked about termination fees twice.
What Maya told me is that they came back with a rate review and a new terminal bundle for the front desks, on a longer contract.

trigger.insight: The trigger was a board-level churn number. Once someone split voluntary cancellations from failed cards, the failed-card bucket was bigger than expected. That is a problem Corelane found in its own data, not one we pitched. The size of the bucket is the rep's unsure recollection, not a confirmed figure.
trigger.messaging: Frame the pitch around the hidden involuntary-churn bucket and how to measure it. Don't use a share-of-churn number until it is confirmed from the board deck.

decider.insight: The rep first named Maya, the head of digital who ran the evaluation, as the decider. When the interviewer pressed, it turned out the controller's signature was needed and the contract sat with him for two weeks. Maya was the champion and Greg the gatekeeper. Our messaging so far has been aimed at Maya's concerns.
decider.messaging: Build for two audiences: the champion who owns the problem and the finance approver who needs numbers on their own data and the cost of leaving.

competitor.insight: Global is the incumbent, in through the studio software. Its response was a rate review plus a terminal bundle on a longer contract, all relayed secondhand by Maya. After that meeting the questions moved from failed payments and retries to readers, studio-software compatibility, contract term and exit cost. Global pulled the conversation toward hardware and lock-in, which is where we are weakest. That Global was 'rattled' is only the rep's guess.
competitor.messaging: Expect the incumbent to reframe the deal around hardware and contract. Prepare answers on reader compatibility and switching cost so they don't dominate.

message.insight: The reaction came from a customer-specific demonstration of recoverable failed renewals, not from any claim. Silence met the global opener, which didn't fit a US and Canada footprint, and 'unified commerce' was read as a hardware question. Our M1 and M3 lines don't map to this buyer's vocabulary.
message.messaging: Move from claims to demonstrations on the customer's data. Drop the global opener for domestic subscription buyers and replace 'unified commerce' with concrete front-desk language.

decided.insight: The sequence is two weeks of silence on the paper, then the data session, then a signature four days later. The rep admits they expected to be there only to pressure the incumbent. The turn followed the controller's request for the spreadsheet, though the rep's timing of 'won' is a retrospective read and the data session is not proven to be the sole cause. The deal also closed narrower than the pitch: online billing now, studios later.
decided.messaging: Make the data session a standard early step, aimed at the finance approver, rather than a late rescue.

gaps.insight: The gap is the front desk: our reader working inside their studio management software on a single screen. We couldn't show it live, only through a partner's demo after the fact, not in their own setup. Global still processes at the front desk, and phase two has no date and depends on the partner piece. The in-store half of our positioning is unproven for this customer, and the incumbent keeps the door open there.
gaps.messaging: Don't make in-store claims for studio-software customers until the integration can be shown in the customer's environment. Treat the partner demo as a proof asset we need to have ready earlier.

language.insight: The interviewer was cut off before finishing this question and the rep deferred it to Slack. The only customer phrase on record is Maya's line from the trigger. 'The studio managers will revolt' is her wording about front-desk screens, not about the core problem. Greg's own words are entirely missing.
language.messaging: Use 'members who never meant to leave' only as a test phrase until the full wording is collected, ideally Greg's as well as Maya's.

gaps.question: What exact words did they use for their problem?
gaps.follow_up: Ask over Slack for verbatim phrases from Maya and Greg, in emails or the board deck, and note which are quoted and which paraphrased.

gaps.question: How big was the failed-card bucket of churn?
gaps.follow_up: Get the actual figure from Maya's board deck, with her permission to cite it, instead of the rep's 'a third, don't quote me'.

gaps.question: Is there a date for phase two (studio front desks)?
gaps.follow_up: Find out what the partner integration needs and who owns the timeline, and whether Global's longer-contract offer is still live with the studios.

gaps.question: What did Greg himself say about why he signed, and how were his termination-fee questions answered?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep what was said back on term and exit costs, and whether Greg can be asked directly why he signed.

close.rep_takeaway: The rep named the champion as the decider until pressed. Ask 'whose signature is on it?' early in every deal and aim at that person from the first meeting, not only at the person running the evaluation.
